1	# Entity-Anchored Contrastive Alignment for Cross-Lingual Knowledge Conductivity
2	
3	## Description
4	EACA is a continued pretraining method that introduces InfoNCE contrastive loss on entity-span hidden states alongside standard next-token prediction, targeting entity-level cross-lingual knowledge conductivity — a capability that CLiKA (NAACL 2024) established is not substantially improved by existing multilingual pretraining or instruction tuning (XRR < 0.01). Unlike CCL-XCoT (sentence/paragraph-level contrastive CPT) and Liu & Niehues (ACL 2025, sentence-level middle-layer contrastive fine-tuning), EACA anchors contrastive pairs to Wikidata QIDs using FactNet's 1.7B entity-grounded atomic facts, operating at the entity level — the granularity empirically shown to be the bottleneck for cross-lingual consistency (entity alignment correlates at r > 0.7 with consistency, arXiv:2510.10280). This extends KBioXLM's (EMNLP Findings 2023) precedent of multi-granularity entity alignment in multilingual pretraining from encoder-based masking objectives in a specialized domain to explicit contrastive alignment in decoder-only LLMs for general-domain conductivity. Entity spans are marked with LEIA-style [ENT]/[/ENT] tokens using DaMuEL (12.3B QID-annotated tokens across 53 languages) as the primary annotation source for 10 of 13 target languages, supplemented by a Wikipedia wikilinks-to-QID extraction pipeline for the 3 uncovered Tier 3 languages (SW/YO/KM) and mReFinED entity linking for non-hyperlinked mention gap-filling, with 1.5-2 weeks budgeted for preprocessing. Representations are extracted via mean-pooling at middle layers (~layer 16, validated via Phase 0 sweep). The proposal explicitly addresses the script barrier identified by Ifergan et al. (NAACL Findings 2025) and Bandarkar et al. (arXiv:2603.17070): script similarity dominates representation sharing (~37.6% same-script CKR vs. <10-20% cross-script), but entity priming disproportionately helps cross-script transfer, motivating entity-level alignment as targeting the right bottleneck. Cross-script QID pairs receive transliteration-augmented entity markers (e.g., [ENT]北京 (Beijing)[/ENT]), inspired by TransliCo (ACL 2024), with mandatory script-grouped evaluation (same-script vs. cross-script gains). Stratified batch construction uses 128-256 entities per batch with class-aware false-negative masking, type-aware hard negatives (~50% same-type entities via Wikidata P31 properties, following Robinson et al. ICLR 2021), and asymmetric positive sets for entities with uneven language coverage (K_min = 3 languages per QID). Joint optimization (L_NTP + λ·L_contrastive, λ=0.1 with warmup) includes gradient conflict monitoring: cosine similarity between NTP and contrastive gradients is tracked every 100 steps, with PCGrad (Yu et al., NeurIPS 2020) activated if conflicts exceed 30% of steps, and GradNorm (Chen et al., ICML 2018) for dynamic λ adjustment if gradient magnitudes diverge beyond 10:1. Inverse-frequency weighting prioritizes low-resource entity-facts. Catastrophic forgetting is mitigated through LoRA (rank 64) on middle layers (10-22), 15% general-domain replay, and cosine LR scheduling. A tiered language selection spans 13 languages across ~7 scripts: Tier 1 (EN/ZH/JA/DE), Tier 2 (AR/HI/TR/ID/VI/TH), Tier 3 (SW/YO/KM), with mandatory Phase 0 FactNet coverage audit and contingency replacements. Phase 0 pilot (500M tokens, 5 languages spanning ≥3 scripts, ~130 H100 hours) includes baselines against sentence-level contrastive (CCL-XCoT), middle-layer sentence contrastive (Liu & Niehues), masking-based entity alignment (KBioXLM-style adaptation), LEIA augmentation, and standard CPT, plus layer sweep, gradient analysis, and script-grouped evaluation. Six key novelties: (1) entity-level contrastive anchoring vs. sentence-level, (2) structured knowledge grounding via FactNet QIDs vs. parallel text, (3) frequency-aware weighting, (4) joint NTP+contrastive optimization with gradient conflict monitoring at entity level during CPT, (5) script-aware transliteration augmentation for cross-script entity alignment, (6) direct targeting of CLiKA's conductivity gap with script-stratified evaluation.
5	
6	## Core Problem
7	Can entity-level contrastive alignment — anchored to Wikidata QIDs and grounded in FactNet's structured atomic facts — improve cross-lingual knowledge conductivity (as defined by CLiKA's XRR metric, Gao et al. NAACL 2024) more effectively than sentence/paragraph-level contrastive continued pretraining (e.g., CCL-XCoT) or sentence-level middle-layer alignment (Liu & Niehues, ACL 2025)? CLiKA established that neither multilingual pretraining nor instruction tuning substantially improves conductivity, with XRR scores below 0.01 for most non-English languages. EACA hypothesizes that this conductivity barrier persists because prior methods align at sentence/document granularity — conflating entity-specific factual knowledge with syntactic and discourse-level variation — whereas factual knowledge is inherently structured around entities (subject-property-object triples). A critical complication, identified by Ifergan et al. (NAACL Findings 2025) and Bandarkar et al. (arXiv:2603.17070), is that script similarity is the dominant factor in cross-lingual representation sharing: high behavioral consistency does not imply shared internal representation for cross-script language pairs, and script match — not language family — is the primary predictor of knowledge transfer failure. Crucially, however, Bandarkar et al.'s entity priming experiment shows that providing source-language entity names disproportionately improves cross-script transfer, directly implicating entity-level mapping failure as the mechanism behind the script barrier. This suggests that entity-level contrastive alignment targets the right bottleneck, but that cross-script entity alignment requires additional support (e.g., transliteration augmentation) beyond what same-script entity alignment needs. EACA therefore addresses a two-level problem: (1) entity-level alignment as the fundamental unit of factual knowledge transfer, and (2) script-aware strategies to bridge the representation gap across writing systems.
8	
9	## Opportunity
10	CCL-XCoT (EMNLP 2025 Findings) demonstrates that contrastive continued pretraining reduces cross-lingual hallucination by up to 62% but operates at sentence/paragraph granularity with parallel text. Liu & Niehues (ACL 2025) show that middle-layer contrastive alignment (layer 16 of 32 in LLaMA-3-8B) significantly improves cross-lingual transfer for downstream tasks, but again at sentence-level granularity and for task-specific fine-tuning rather than factual consistency. CLiKA (NAACL 2024) reveals a critical gap: existing multilingual pretraining and instruction tuning improve surface-level consistency but fail to improve knowledge conductivity (XRR < 0.01), suggesting that fundamentally different alignment granularity is needed. Meanwhile, FactNet (arXiv:2602.03417, Feb 2026) provides 1.7B entity-grounded atomic facts across 316 Wikipedia editions with Wikidata QID linking — enabling entity-level contrastive pairs grounded in structured knowledge. Entity Lens (BlackboxNLP 2025) confirms that decoder LLMs develop entity-specific internal mechanisms to represent multi-token entities. Liu et al. (EMNLP 2025 Findings) show that cross-lingual transfer is frequency-driven, with low-frequency facts benefiting most. Critically, recent evidence from entity-level alignment analysis (Liu, Wang et al., arXiv:2510.10280) demonstrates that cross-lingual factual consistency correlates strongly with entity alignment (Pearson r > 0.7), with over 99% of consistent facts exhibiting successful entity alignment — providing direct empirical motivation for entity-level rather than sentence-level contrastive objectives. Marco et al. ('Unveiling LLMs', arXiv:2404.03623) further establish that factual knowledge about subject entities concentrates in middle layers (L5-L21 for LLaMA-2-7B). KBioXLM (EMNLP Findings 2023) provides an important precedent: it demonstrated that multi-granularity knowledge alignment (entity masking, relation masking, passage relation prediction) during continued pretraining of XLM-R yields +20 F1 points on cross-lingual zero-shot biomedical tasks, establishing entity-anchored alignment as effective — but using masking-based reconstruction on encoders rather than contrastive loss on decoder LLMs, and targeting downstream task transfer rather than factual conductivity. Ifergan et al. (NAACL Findings 2025) reveal a deeper challenge: using knowledge editing as a probe for representation sharing, they find script similarity is the dominant factor (same-script CKR ~37.6% in Mistral; cross-script <10-20%), and that behavioral consistency diverges sharply from representation sharing for cross-script pairs. Bandarkar et al. (arXiv:2603.17070, March 2026) confirm this with regression analysis showing script match as the primary predictor after controlling for model capability and question difficulty (~13% accuracy gap), but critically, their entity priming experiment shows that providing source-language entity names disproportionately improves cross-script questions — directly implicating entity mapping as the bottleneck. TransliCo (ACL 2024) demonstrates that transliteration-based contrastive learning bridges script barriers using only 5% of training data on encoders. DaMuEL (2023) provides 12.3B tokens with QID-linked entity annotations across 53 languages, enabling efficient preprocessing for 10 of EACA's 13 target languages. The opportunity is to combine these insights — entity-level anchoring + structured knowledge grounding + middle-layer extraction + inverse-frequency weighting + script-aware strategies — into a contrastive CPT method that targets the specific granularity (entities), representation layer (middle), data regime (low-frequency facts), and script barriers where current methods demonstrably fall short.
11	
12	## Related Work / Landscape
13	The cross-lingual factual consistency landscape spans several complementary approaches. CCL-XCoT (EMNLP 2025 Findings) is the primary baseline, employing InfoNCE symmetric contrastive loss during continued pretraining with a sentence-to-paragraph curriculum on Gemma-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B using LoRA on layers 9-19/11-22, reducing hallucination by 62%, but operating at sentence/paragraph granularity without entity grounding or frequency weighting. Liu & Niehues (ACL 2025) represent the closest methodological precedent for contrastive alignment: they apply contrastive loss on mean-pooled sentence representations at middle layers (specifically layer 16 of 32 for LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct) during task-specific fine-tuning with LoRA (rank 8), demonstrating +1.5 F1 on slot filling and +1.5 BLEU on MT across 35 languages — however, they use sentence-level alignment with alternating (not joint) task/alignment training, target downstream task transfer rather than factual consistency, use parallel text rather than structured knowledge, and include no frequency weighting. EACA differentiates from Liu & Niehues on five axes: (1) entity-level rather than sentence-level granularity, (2) continued pretraining for factual consistency rather than task-specific fine-tuning, (3) FactNet-grounded contrastive pairs rather than parallel text, (4) joint NTP+contrastive objective rather than alternating training, and (5) inverse-frequency weighting for underrepresented facts. KBioXLM (Geng et al., EMNLP Findings 2023, arXiv:2311.11564) is an important precedent for multi-granularity entity-anchored alignment in multilingual pretraining. It performs continued pretraining on XLM-R using three alignment objectives grounded in UMLS biomedical knowledge: entity masking (code-switching entity mentions across EN-CN and predicting masked entity tokens via MLM cross-entropy), relation masking (masking relation tokens in subject-predicate-object triples), and passage relation prediction (3-way classification on aligned EN-CN Wikipedia passages). KBioXLM achieves +20 F1 points on cross-lingual zero-shot biomedical NER/RE. EACA extends this paradigm along four dimensions: (a) decoder-only LLMs vs. encoder (XLM-R), requiring contrastive loss on hidden states rather than masking-based reconstruction, since decoder LLMs lack bidirectional context for effective mask prediction; (b) general domain vs. biomedical, using FactNet's 1.7B facts across 316 editions vs. UMLS's specialized ontology; (c) explicit contrastive alignment (InfoNCE) vs. implicit alignment through masking, directly optimizing cross-lingual entity representation similarity rather than relying on the prediction bottleneck; (d) conductivity metric (CLiKA's XRR) vs. downstream task transfer, targeting the specific capability that prior methods fail to improve. CLiKA (Gao et al., NAACL 2024) provides the diagnostic framework: they define knowledge conductivity as the Cross-Retrieval Ratio (XRR) — retrieving knowledge learned in one language using another — and find that neither multilingual pretraining nor instruction tuning substantially improves XRR (scores < 0.01 for most non-English languages), with no concrete solutions proposed. The entity-level alignment analysis (Liu, Wang et al., arXiv:2510.10280) provides strong empirical support: cross-lingual consistency correlates with entity alignment at r > 0.7, and their SubInj method yields +14-32% recall and +17-44% consistency gains, but only at inference time; EACA aims to achieve this alignment at training time. On the script barrier dimension, Ifergan et al. ('Beneath the Surface of Consistency', NAACL Findings 2025, arXiv:2408.10646) demonstrate via knowledge editing probes on 7 decoder LLMs (7B scale) that script similarity is the dominant factor in cross-lingual knowledge representation sharing (CKR): same-script Latin pairs show ~37.6% average CKR in Mistral, while cross-script pairs show <10-20% transfer; crucially, they find that high behavioral consistency (CKC) does not imply shared representation for cross-script pairs, with E[NCL] consistently exceeding E[NTL]. Even targeted language extension pretraining achieves only marginal cross-script CKR improvement. Bandarkar et al. ('Large Reasoning Models Struggle to Transfer Parametric Knowledge Across Scripts', arXiv:2603.17070, March 2026) confirm via regression analysis on ECLeKTic and MultiLoKo that script match — not language family — is the primary predictor of knowledge transfer failure (~13% accuracy gap), but their entity priming experiment reveals that providing source-language entity names disproportionately improves cross-script questions, directly implicating entity mapping as the cross-script bottleneck. TransliCo (Liu et al., ACL 2024, arXiv:2401.06620) addresses script barriers through transliteration contrastive modeling (TCM), fine-tuning Glot500-m on 5% of data with Latin transliterations as contrastive targets, producing Furina which outperforms Glot500-m on cross-script zero-shot transfer — but operates on encoders at sentence level without entity grounding. Transliteration-based post-training alignment (Moosa et al., EMNLP Findings 2024, arXiv:2406.19759) achieves up to 50% improvement on cross-script English-centric transfer with even larger gains for non-English sources. EACA incorporates this insight by adding transliteration-augmented entity contrastive pairs for cross-script language combinations as a complementary mechanism. NeighXLM (EMNLP 2025 Findings) introduces neighbor-augmented contrastive pretraining for low-resource languages without parallel data, but targets general cross-lingual transfer rather than entity-specific factual consistency. PreAlign (EMNLP 2024) uses code-switching pretraining with word-level alignment but lacks entity anchoring. CrossIC-PT (EMNLP 2025) interleaves bilingual Wikipedia content without entity-level grounding. LEIA (ACL Findings 2024) inserts English entity names with [translate]/[/translate] markers during continued pretraining of decoder LLMs, improving cross-lingual transfer but without contrastive loss or frequency weighting. EntityCS (EMNLP Findings 2022) performs entity-centric code switching with Wikidata but is limited to encoder-only models. Entity Lens (BlackboxNLP 2025) reveals that decoder LLMs develop entity-specific mechanisms to represent and manipulate multi-token entities via task vectors. The middle-layer factual knowledge claim is supported by Liu & Niehues (ACL 2025) showing layer 16 of 32 has strongest cross-lingual retrieval alignment, and Marco et al. (arXiv:2404.03623) demonstrating via dynamic knowledge graphs that middle layers (L5-L21) encode comprehensive factual knowledge while late layers show 90%+ degradation. ELO (arXiv:2601.03648, Jan 2026) demonstrates efficient layer-specific optimization with 6.46x speedup from selective middle-layer updates. FactNet (arXiv:2602.03417) provides 1.7B entity-grounded facts across 316 Wikipedia editions with significant coverage skew. CLM-Bench (arXiv:2601.17397) shows edit vectors are nearly orthogonal across languages, further motivating entity-level alignment. DCO (arXiv:2603.04678, March 2026) proposes DPO-inspired post-hoc consistency optimization, complementary to pretraining-time methods. Veitsman et al. (arXiv:2603.18863, March 2026) find that sentence-level contrastive alignment fails for token-level tasks in XLM-R encoders, supporting entity-level approaches for entity-centric tasks. Cultural knowledge asymmetry research (ACL 2025) confirms that frequency drives cross-lingual transferability.
14	
15	## Approach
16	EACA adds an InfoNCE contrastive loss on entity-span hidden states to the standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective during continued pretraining. The method comprises five integrated components: entity preprocessing, entity-level contrastive alignment, script-aware augmentation, stratified batch construction, and joint optimization with gradient monitoring.
17	
18	**1. Entity Preprocessing Pipeline.** Entity boundary annotation uses a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 (primary): DaMuEL (2023), which provides 12.3B QID-annotated tokens across 53 languages (CC BY-SA), is used directly for the 10 target languages it covers (EN/ZH/JA/DE/AR/HI/TR/ID/VI/TH). DaMuEL provides start/end token indices per entity mention with Wikidata QID links, extracted from Wikipedia wikilinks and expanded via lemmatization and alias matching (~17% recall gain over raw wikilinks). Stage 2 (Tier 3 gap-filling): For the 3 Tier 3 languages not covered by DaMuEL (SW/YO/KM), a lightweight Wikipedia wikilinks extraction pipeline resolves hyperlinks to QIDs via Wikidata sitelinks (~50-60% mention coverage). mReFinED (EMNLP Findings 2023), which is 44-60x faster than comparable entity linkers, is applied as a second pass on high-resource languages to annotate non-hyperlinked entity mentions where higher recall is needed. Entity boundaries are marked with LEIA-style [ENT]/[/ENT] tokens around linked mentions. Preprocessing budget: 1.5-2 weeks engineering time, ~2-4 GPU-days on A100 for mReFinED gap-filling, ~24-48 CPU-hours for wikilinks extraction across Tier 3 languages. This pipeline is on the critical path and must complete before Phase 0.
19	
20	**2. Entity-Level Contrastive Alignment.** Entity representations are extracted via mean-pooling over hidden states within the [ENT]...[/ENT] span at a designated middle layer (defaulting to layer 16 for 32-layer models based on Liu & Niehues' ACL 2025 finding and Marco et al.'s analysis; validated via Phase 0 sweep over layers 12-20), with loss propagation blocked on boundary markers themselves. Contrastive pairs are constructed per QID from FactNet: positive pairs consist of atomic fact descriptions for the same QID across languages, while negatives come from different QIDs within the same batch (detailed in Component 4). Inverse-frequency weighting assigns higher contrastive loss weight to facts with lower cross-lingual FactNet coverage, directly targeting low-resource facts where CLiKA's conductivity analysis shows the largest gap.
21	
22	Theoretical motivation for entity-level granularity: Three converging lines of evidence support entity-level over sentence-level contrastive alignment for factual consistency: (1) Entity alignment analysis (arXiv:2510.10280) demonstrates Pearson r > 0.7 between entity alignment and cross-lingual consistency, with >99% of consistent facts showing successful entity alignment — establishing entities as the bottleneck for consistency; (2) CLM-Bench's finding that cross-lingual edit vectors are nearly orthogonal implies that factual knowledge editing, which operates at entity-level (subject-property-object triples), requires entity-aligned representations rather than sentence-aligned ones; (3) CLiKA's failure result — that sentence/document-level pretraining and instruction tuning do not improve conductivity — suggests that coarser-grained alignment conflates entity-specific factual knowledge with syntactic and discourse-level variation, diluting the alignment signal.
23	
24	**3. Script Barrier Mitigation.** EACA's 13 target languages span ~7 scripts (Latin: EN/DE/TR/ID/VI/SW/YO; CJK: ZH/JA; Arabic: AR; Devanagari: HI; Thai: TH; Khmer: KM). Ifergan et al. (NAACL Findings 2025) demonstrate that cross-lingual representation sharing (CKR) clusters strongly by script family (~37.6% same-script CKR vs. <10-20% cross-script in Mistral-7B), and Bandarkar et al. (arXiv:2603.17070) confirm script match as the primary predictor of transfer failure (~13% gap). This poses a genuine risk that entity-level contrastive alignment may primarily improve same-script entity alignment while showing limited gains for cross-script pairs. However, two findings provide grounds for cautious optimism: (a) Bandarkar et al.'s entity priming experiment shows source-language entity names disproportionately improve cross-script transfer, implicating entity mapping — not script-level representation — as the cross-script bottleneck for factual knowledge; (b) TransliCo (ACL 2024) demonstrates that transliteration-based contrastive learning bridges script barriers on encoders using only 5% of training data. EACA therefore incorporates a script-aware augmentation strategy: for cross-script QID pairs (e.g., EN-ZH, EN-AR, EN-HI, EN-TH, EN-KM), entity mentions in non-Latin scripts are supplemented with Latin transliterations appended within the [ENT] boundary (e.g., [ENT]北京 (Beijing)[/ENT]), providing a lexical bridge for the contrastive objective. This is tested as an ablation (EACA vs. EACA+translit) to isolate the contribution of transliteration augmentation beyond entity-level alignment. The evaluation plan includes mandatory script-grouped analysis: same-script entity alignment gains (Latin-Latin, CJK-CJK) vs. cross-script gains (Latin-CJK, Latin-Arabic, Latin-Devanagari, etc.), reporting both entity cosine similarity and downstream factual consistency metrics separately for each script-pair category. If Phase 0 reveals that cross-script entity alignment gains are <50% of same-script gains despite transliteration augmentation, this will be explicitly reported as a limitation and the analysis will quantify what fraction of EACA's overall conductivity improvement comes from same-script vs. cross-script alignment.
25	
26	**4. Stratified Batch Construction with Type-Aware Hard Negatives.** Effective contrastive learning is highly sensitive to negative quality (Robinson et al., ICLR 2021). EACA uses stratified mini-batching: each batch contains K_batch = 128-256 unique QIDs, with all available language instances per QID forming the positive set (asymmetric positive sets accommodate QIDs present in only 2-3 languages without dropping them). Minimum language coverage per QID is K_min = 3 languages; QIDs with fewer than 3 language instances are filtered during preprocessing. Class-Aware Masking (CAM) ensures that all instances of the same QID are excluded from the InfoNCE denominator, preventing false-negative contamination. For hard negative mining, type-aware stratification ensures ~50% of in-batch negatives share the anchor entity's Wikidata type (e.g., Q5/human, Q515/city, Q4830453/organization) — forcing the model to discriminate on fine-grained entity identity rather than coarse type. This is implemented via Wikidata instance-of (P31) properties, grouping entities into 8-10 macro-types for sampling. The remaining ~50% are random negatives for diversity. Batch composition is balanced across script families to ensure cross-script contrastive signals appear in every batch. The InfoNCE loss for entity e with QID q is: L_entity(q) = -log[exp(sim(h_q^i, h_q^j)/τ) / (exp(sim(h_q^i, h_q^j)/τ) + Σ_{k≠q} exp(sim(h_q^i, h_k)/τ))], where h_q^i, h_q^j are entity representations from different languages for the same QID, and h_k are representations from different QIDs, with τ = 0.07 as the temperature (tuned in Phase 0 over {0.05, 0.07, 0.1}).
27	
28	**5. Joint Optimization with Gradient Monitoring.** The joint objective is L_total = L_NTP + λ * L_entity_contrastive, with λ initialized at 0.1 (following guidance from headless LM work showing λ ∈ [0.01, 0.1] is appropriate for contrastive + generation joint training during CPT). A potential tension exists: NTP learns language-specific token distributions while contrastive loss pulls entity representations together across languages. Unlike Liu & Niehues' alternating approach, EACA uses joint optimization to ensure entity alignment co-adapts with the language modeling objective — but addresses gradient conflict risk through three mechanisms: (a) Phase 0 gradient analysis: cosine similarity between ∇L_NTP and ∇L_entity_contrastive is computed every 100 steps on the shared LoRA parameters. If gradient cosine similarity is negative for >30% of monitored steps, PCGrad projection (Yu et al., NeurIPS 2020) is applied — projecting the contrastive gradient onto the normal plane of the NTP gradient to eliminate destructive interference. (b) GradNorm (Chen et al., ICML 2018) is implemented as an optional dynamic λ adjustment mechanism: if the gradient magnitude ratio between the two losses drifts beyond 10:1, GradNorm normalizes to equalize learning rates. (c) λ warmup: contrastive loss weight ramps linearly from 0 to λ_target over the first 10% of training steps, allowing NTP to stabilize before contrastive pressure is introduced. Phase 0 reports gradient conflict frequency, cosine similarity distribution, and whether PCGrad/GradNorm activation was required — this informs the full training configuration. If gradient conflicts are severe (>50% of steps) even with PCGrad, the fallback is alternating optimization (NTP steps → contrastive steps per batch) following Liu & Niehues' validated approach.
29	
30	Catastrophic forgetting is mitigated through three mechanisms: (a) LoRA (rank 64) applied to middle layers only (layers 10-22), following CCL-XCoT's selective layer approach and ELO's findings that first/last layers are critical for general capabilities; (b) 15% general-domain English replay data mixed into training batches; (c) cosine learning rate schedule with linear warmup (peak LR 2e-5). Language selection follows a tiered strategy: Tier 1 comprises 4 anchor languages (EN/ZH/JA/DE, >1M entity-fact pairs), Tier 2 includes 6 mid-resource languages (AR/HI/TR/ID/VI/TH, 100K-1M pairs), and Tier 3 covers 3 low-resource languages (SW/YO/KM). Tier 3 viability assessment based on Wikipedia article counts (SW: ~117K, YO: ~37K, KM: ~12K) and FactNet's 0.36 low-resource yield rate estimates approximately 50K-200K entity-fact pairs for Swahili, 15K-60K for Yoruba, and 5K-25K for Khmer. None of the Tier 3 languages are covered by DaMuEL, so all three rely on the Wikipedia wikilinks extraction pipeline (Stage 2 above). A mandatory FactNet coverage audit in Phase 0 will report exact entity-fact pair counts for all 13 languages; minimum viable threshold is set at 10K entity-fact pairs per language (sufficient for contrastive batching at size 128-256 with adequate negative diversity). If any Tier 3 language falls below threshold, contingency replacements include Bengali (BN, ~157K Wikipedia articles), Tagalog (TL, ~115K articles), or Hausa (HA, ~8K articles but stronger NLP benchmark coverage). Languages below 25K pairs receive LEIA-style English entity augmentation to supplement contrastive pairs.
31	
32	Phase 0 pilot uses 500M tokens across 5 languages (3 Tier-1 + 2 Tier-2, selected to span at least 3 scripts for script barrier analysis) for approximately 130 H100 hours, with baselines including: (a) CCL-XCoT-style sentence-level contrastive CPT, (b) Liu & Niehues-style middle-layer sentence-level contrastive alignment (the closest methodological comparison, testing entity-level vs. sentence-level at the same middle layer), (c) LEIA-style entity augmentation without contrastive loss, (d) standard CPT, and (e) KBioXLM-style entity masking adaptation (masking [ENT]-bounded tokens and predicting via NTP, without contrastive loss — testing contrastive vs. masking-based entity alignment on decoders). Phase 0 additionally includes: a layer sweep (layers 12, 14, 16, 18, 20) to empirically determine optimal entity extraction depth; gradient conflict analysis (cosine similarity monitoring, PCGrad activation rate); and script-grouped entity alignment analysis (same-script vs. cross-script gains). Go/no-go criteria require entity cosine similarity improvement of at least 0.05, BMLAMA-53 consistency improvement of at least 2 points, no TyDiQA degradation beyond 1 point, AND gradient conflict rate below 50% (with or without PCGrad). 1	# Language Feature Anchoring: Preventing Cross-Lingual Collapse in RLVR via Entanglement-Aware SAE-Guided Preservation
2	
3	## Description
4	During RLVR training for reasoning, chain-of-thought systematically collapses to English — even though RL preserves overall representational geometry 4–15× better than SFT. Five independent studies converge on middle-to-late transformer layers as the locus of language identity in Qwen-family and comparable models: LinguaMap finds language emergence at ~86% depth in Qwen-3-32B; SAE-LAPE finds 52% of language-specific SAE features at 75–94% depth; Causal Language Control achieves 90%+ steering at 55–86% depth; SASFT confirms late-layer primacy for Qwen3; and the NeurIPS 2025 disentanglement paper shows top-layer language features are essential across Qwen-2.5/3 models. ReasonXL's early-layer finding (layers 6–8) appears specific to SmolLM3-3B. We resolve the stability paradox — global geometry preserved yet collapse occurs — by hypothesizing that GRPO advantage signals create concentrated drift at language-critical features in these middle-to-late layers, even as overall representations stay intact. We propose Entanglement-Aware Language Feature Anchoring (LFA): using Qwen-Scope pre-trained SAEs to identify and classify language-specific features at the target layers of Qwen3-8B into three tiers — pure language features (hard anchored via MSE), dual-function features carrying both language and reasoning information (directionally anchored: penalizing drift toward English while allowing within-language reasoning adaptation), and pure reasoning features (unconstrained). A prerequisite Phase 0 performs full-depth language feature census, GRPO-induced drift analysis, entanglement measurement, and activation patching across all 36 layers to determine which layers to target and what entanglement profile exists — this characterization is itself a contribution. The entanglement-aware formulation is motivated by the NeurIPS 2025 finding that language-specific ablation at middle layers improves reasoning (+1.27pp on Qwen-3-8B), suggesting meaningful separation exists even where both processes operate. We articulate three falsifiable predictions distinguishing LFA from reward methods: (P1) post-training robustness — LFA-trained models maintain >90% LC after 100 additional reward-free GRPO steps, while reward-trained models degrade, because LFA fixes the representation rather than relying on persistent corrective signals; (P2) unseen language transfer — LFA achieves higher LC on held-out languages because it anchors general routing features; (P3) training efficiency — LFA with accuracy-only reward reaches 95% LC faster than multi-reward approaches because it prevents initial collapse. Evaluation on MGSM/MGSM-Pro across 10 languages compares against vanilla GRPO, M-Thinker, SP3F, and SASFT+GRPO. Stratified expectations: LFA primarily benefits mid-resource languages; for low-resource languages, understanding failures dominate and we test a combined LFA + Selective Translation condition.
5	
6	## Core Problem
7	During reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for reasoning, chain-of-thought systematically collapses to English — especially for low-resource languages (Ukrainian: 0.3% target word ratio after 250 GRPO steps). Recent methods achieve strong results across different resource levels: M-Thinker and TRIT reach near-perfect language consistency for mid-to-high-resource languages, while SP3F demonstrates that RL with privileged pairwise judges can improve low-resource languages (Swahili MGSM: 0.8% → 20.5%, Bengali: 45.8% → 57.6%). However, all existing approaches operate at the reward level (adding language consistency rewards or privileged judges) without addressing the representational mechanism driving collapse. Meanwhile, converging evidence from five independent studies locates language identity features in middle-to-late transformer layers for Qwen-family and comparable models: LinguaMap (arXiv:2601.20009) finds language emergence at ~86% depth in Qwen-3-32B; SAE-LAPE (arXiv:2507.11230) finds language-specific SAE features predominantly in middle-to-final layers with 52% concentrating in the top quarter; Causal Language Control (arXiv:2507.13410) achieves 90%+ language steering at 55–86% depth in Gemma-2; SASFT (ICLR 2026) shows code-switching reduction 'generally deteriorates as we move towards earlier layers' for Qwen3; and the NeurIPS 2025 disentanglement paper finds 'preserving top-layer language features remains essential' for linguistic fidelity across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3 models. A critical paradox exists: RL preserves overall representational geometry 4–15× better than SFT (KL 0.084 vs 0.372), yet cross-lingual collapse still occurs abruptly within 100–250 GRPO steps. This suggests collapse is not caused by wholesale representation destruction but by targeted drift at language-critical features in the model's middle-to-late layers — a mechanism that reward-level interventions can mask but not mechanistically resolve. The key challenge for training-time anchoring at these layers is language-reasoning feature entanglement: language features at the same depth as reasoning computations may carry dual roles, making naive anchoring risky. Can entanglement-aware SAE-guided anchoring during GRPO prevent cross-lingual collapse while preserving reasoning quality, even at layers where language and reasoning features coexist?
8	
9	## Opportunity
10	Five converging developments create a unique opportunity: (1) Cross-lingual collapse (arXiv:2506.05850) reveals that GRPO advantage signals systematically favor English reasoning trajectories, causing abrupt language switching — but the paper provides only behavioral analysis, not mechanistic explanation. (2) Five independent studies converge on middle-to-late layers as the locus of language identity in modern LLMs: LinguaMap finds language emergence at ~86% depth in Qwen-3-32B (layer 55 of 64); SAE-LAPE finds language-specific features predominantly in middle-to-final layers across Llama-3.2-1B/Llama-3.1-8B/Gemma-2-2B/9B, with peak concentration at ~87–94% depth; Causal Language Control achieves peak language steering at 55–86% depth in Gemma-2-9B via single-feature SAE intervention; SASFT confirms late-layer primacy for Qwen3; and the NeurIPS 2025 disentanglement paper shows top-layer language features are essential across Qwen-2.5/3 models. ReasonXL (arXiv:2604.12378) found language routing at layers 6–8 (~17–23% depth) in SmolLM3-3B, but this appears model-specific — the paper explicitly notes 'generalization to larger scales remains to be verified.' This model-dependent variation is itself scientifically interesting and Phase 0 will characterize which pattern Qwen3-8B follows. (3) SASFT (ICLR 2026) demonstrates that SAE-identified language features can be constrained during SFT to reduce code-switching by 50–100%, validating the mechanistic intervention principle — but only for SFT, not RL, and using a suppression formulation that does not account for entanglement with reasoning features. (4) Qwen-Scope (arXiv:2605.11887) provides pre-trained SAEs for Qwen3-8B across all 36 layers with monolinguality scoring infrastructure, and mentions SAE signals for RL — but no published work has instantiated this for cross-lingual collapse prevention. (5) The NeurIPS 2025 disentanglement paper demonstrates that language-specific ablation at middle layers IMPROVES multilingual reasoning (Qwen-3-8B: 84.15% → 85.42% on MGSM), suggesting meaningful separation exists even at layers where both processes operate — this is critical for LFA's feasibility because it implies anchoring language features will not automatically damage reasoning. Additionally, 'RL Fine-Tunes a Sparse Subnetwork' (NeurIPS 2025) shows RL modifies only 5–30% of parameters. The stability paradox — global geometry preserved yet collapse occurs — is resolved by the language drift hypothesis: GRPO's advantage-weighted gradient creates concentrated pressure on language-critical features in the model's language-encoding layers, eroding target-language routing even as overall representations stay intact. Existing reward-level methods (M-Thinker, TRIT, SP3F) treat the symptom without anchoring the cause, which is why they require persistent reward signals. LFA targets exactly this mechanism — and the entanglement-aware formulation addresses the key challenge of anchoring at layers where language and reasoning features coexist. FPO (arXiv:2411.07618, ICML 2025) validates that SAE feature-level constraints during optimization are computationally efficient (17.6% reduction vs TDPO).
11	
12	## Related Work / Landscape
13	**Reward-based methods**: M-Thinker (arXiv:2510.07300) uses LC + CTA rewards during GRPO, achieving 98.29% in-domain language consistency with +6.46pp accuracy on MMATH (7B model, 10 languages), and reports 'excellent generalization on out-of-domain languages.' TRIT (arXiv:2602.05940) integrates translation and reasoning training, outperforming M-Thinker by ~7pp LC&Acc (Qwen3-1.7B/4B, 5 languages, ~100% LC). SP3F / 'Gained in Translation' (arXiv:2601.18722, Jan 2026) uses a two-stage approach on Qwen2.5-7B: SFT on translated English data, then DR.GRPO with privileged pairwise judges (GPT-4o-mini), testing 18 training languages + 8 unseen languages. SP3F achieves 95.35% language fidelity and significant low-resource gains (Swahili MGSM: 0.8% → 20.5%, Bengali: 45.8% → 57.6%), with positive transfer to unseen languages. M2A (arXiv:2507.05418, ICLR 2026) uses multi-scale multilingual alignment rewards on Qwen2.5-7B, achieving 97.8% LC. PB-RLSVR (arXiv:2509.25543) uses pivot-based semantic rewards. ExpLang (arXiv:2602.21887) uses on-policy thinking language selection. **Critical gap in reward methods**: All operate at the output/reward level, requiring persistent corrective signals during training. A key untested question is post-training robustness: if additional training continues without language rewards, do these methods maintain consistency, or does collapse resume because the internal representation was never fixed? **Representation-location studies (the layer question)**: LinguaMap (arXiv:2601.20009) extends logit lens analysis on Qwen-3-32B (64 layers) and Bloom-7.1B, revealing a three-phase structure: early layers normalize inputs into shared semantic space, middle layers perform task reasoning, and late layers (layer 55+, ~86% depth in Qwen-3-32B) drive language-specific generation. Selective fine-tuning of only the last 2–3 layers achieves >98% language consistency across 6 languages on Qwen-3-32B. SAE-LAPE (arXiv:2507.11230) introduces feature activation probability-based identification of language-specific SAE features across Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B, and Gemma-2-9B. On Llama-3.2-1B (16 layers), 52% of all 540 language-specific features concentrate in layers 12–15 (75–94% depth), with peak at layer 14 (~87% depth). Non-Latin-script languages (Hindi: 142 features, Thai: 70, Japanese: 43) have far more features than Latin-script languages (Spanish: 4, English: 7), suggesting script distance from English correlates with feature count — a finding relevant to stratified evaluation. Causal Language Control (arXiv:2507.13410) uses SAE feature steering on Gemma-2-2B/9B, achieving up to 97.8% (Chinese) and 93.8% (Japanese) language shift success by modifying a single SAE feature. Peak steering effectiveness is at layers 23–36 in Gemma-2-9B (55–86% depth), with layer 29 (~69% depth) as the critical inflection point. Crucially, 'minimal semantic degradation' was observed, suggesting language features at these layers can be manipulated without large reasoning damage. ReasonXL (arXiv:2604.12378) found language identity causally gated at layers 6–8 (~17–23% depth) in SmolLM3-3B via activation patching, but explicitly notes 'experiments are restricted to a single 3B-parameter model... generalization remains to be verified.' **Representation-engineering methods**: SASFT (arXiv:2507.14894, ICLR 2026) constrains SAE-identified language features during SFT via auxiliary loss L_reduce = E[ReLU(f_s(x) − α_j)], achieving 50–100% code-switching reduction across Qwen3/Llama/Gemma. Critically for Qwen3, performance 'generally deteriorates as we move towards earlier layers,' confirming late-layer primacy. The NeurIPS 2025 disentanglement paper ('When Less Language is More,' arXiv:2505.15257) performs SVD-based ablation of language-specific representations at inference, finding: (a) ablation at middle layers IMPROVES reasoning across 10 LLMs on MGSM (Qwen-3-8B: +1.27pp), suggesting meaningful language-reasoning separation exists; (b) 'interventions at the upper layers lead to a sharp drop in both reasoning and response fidelity,' confirming top-layer features are essential; (c) 'middle layers offer the best trade-off between reasoning gains and linguistic coherence.' Qwen-Scope (arXiv:2605.11887) provides pre-trained SAEs for Qwen3-1.7B/8B with monolinguality scoring; language classification F1 >0.90 concentrated in middle-to-late layers. FPO (arXiv:2411.07618, ICML 2025) validates SAE feature-level MSE constraints are computationally efficient. CRL (arXiv:2602.10437) uses SAE features with RL for interpretable steering. LangFIR (arXiv:2604.03532), Neural FOXP2 (arXiv:2602.00945), and MRRE (arXiv:2511.23231) operate only at inference time. 'Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions' (arXiv:2510.07213, EACL 2026) identifies K=100–400 dimensions governing language. 'Why Do Multilingual Reasoning Gaps Emerge' (arXiv:2510.27269) shows understanding failures dominate for low-resource languages (Swahili: 29.3% → 88.0% with understanding intervention). **Gap synthesis**: (a) No work applies SAE-guided language feature constraints to the GRPO training loop. (b) Five studies converge on middle-to-late layers for language features in Qwen-family models, but no work has leveraged this localization for RL-time collapse prevention. (c) The entanglement problem — language features coexisting with reasoning features at the same layers — is identified at inference (NeurIPS 2025) but never addressed for training-time anchoring. (d) Reward-level methods treat symptoms without anchoring representational causes, and their post-training robustness is untested. (e) The interaction between RL's sparse parameter updates and language-critical features at different model depths remains uncharacterized.
14	
15	## Approach
16	**Phase 0 — Language Feature Localization and Entanglement Characterization (prerequisite, ~2.5 weeks)**: Run 250 steps of vanilla GRPO on Qwen3-8B using MGSM training data. Using Qwen-Scope pre-trained SAEs (SAE-Res-Qwen3-8B-Base-W64K-L0_50), conduct four analyses: (A) **Full-depth language feature census**: Compute monolinguality scores for all 64K SAE features at each of the 36 layers. Identify the layers with highest concentration of high-monolinguality features. Based on converging evidence from LinguaMap (~86% depth on Qwen-3-32B), SAE-LAPE (52% of features at 75–94% depth on Llama-3.2-1B), Causal Language Control (peak at 55–86% depth on Gemma-2-9B), and SASFT (late-layer primacy for Qwen3), our **primary hypothesis** is that language features concentrate at layers ~25–34 (69–94% depth) in Qwen3-8B. Our **alternative hypothesis**, based on ReasonXL's finding on SmolLM3-3B, is that an early-mid bottleneck (layers 6–8, ~17–22% depth) exists. Phase 0 determines which pattern Qwen3-8B follows — this is itself a contribution, as no prior work has characterized language feature depth in Qwen3-8B specifically via SAE analysis. (B) **GRPO-induced language feature drift**: Compare feature activations pre/post-GRPO at all 36 layers. Measure drift (Pearson r, Jaccard overlap of top-K active features) specifically for high-monolinguality features vs. low-monolinguality features. **Hypothesis**: Language-critical features at the identified encoding layers show disproportionate drift (>2× vs. non-language features at the same layers), correlating with language consistency loss. (C) **Language-reasoning entanglement measurement**: For each high-monolinguality feature at the target layers, measure its activation on two contrasting data types: (i) monolingual text (FLORES+, 100 sentences per language) and (ii) reasoning traces (MGSM solutions in target languages). Compute a dual-function score: D(s) = min(monolinguality(s), reasoning_activation(s)) where reasoning_activation is the feature's mean activation during reasoning tasks relative to its overall mean. Classify features into three tiers: Tier 1 (pure language): high monolinguality, low reasoning activation (D < 0.3); Tier 2 (dual-function): both high (D ≥ 0.3); Tier 3 (pure reasoning): low monolinguality. Report the overlap ratio: what fraction of high-monolinguality features are also high-reasoning-activation? Based on the NeurIPS 2025 finding that SVD-based language ablation at middle layers improves reasoning (+1.27pp on Qwen-3-8B), we expect meaningful separation — Tier 2 features should be a minority (<30%) of high-monolinguality features. If overlap exceeds 50%, this indicates tight entanglement requiring the full asymmetric loss formulation; if below 20%, simple MSE anchoring on Tier 1 features alone may suffice. (D) **Causal validation via activation patching**: Following ReasonXL's methodology, patch post-GRPO hidden states from specific layers back into the pre-GRPO model. Test at 6 depth zones: layers 1–6, 7–12, 13–18, 19–24, 25–30, 31–36. If patching the zone identified in (A) reproduces the language switch while patching other zones does not, this confirms the causal mechanism. If the early-layer zone (7–12) also shows an effect, Qwen3-8B may have a distributed two-site architecture — a novel finding in itself. **Go/no-go criteria**: If no layer zone shows language-specific drift >1.5× non-language drift AND patching shows no zone-specific language effect, the targeted anchoring hypothesis is falsified → activate contingency (gradient-aware anchoring, see below). **Phase 0 outputs**: (i) identification of 2–4 critical language-encoding layers, (ii) entanglement profile (Tier 1/2/3 feature counts and layer distribution), (iii) reference feature activations f_s^ref, (iv) go/no-go decision with contingency selection if needed. **Phase 1 — Language Feature Identification and Tier Assignment**: Using Qwen-Scope SAEs at the 2–4 target layers from Phase 0 (expected: layers ~25–34), compute monolinguality scores per feature per target language. For each language l, identify S_l = top-K language-specific features, testing K ∈ {50, 100, 200, 400}. Assign each feature to a tier based on Phase 0's entanglement analysis. Compute reference feature activations f_s^ref from the frozen base model on 100 monolingual sentences per language. Since we only need SAEs at 2–4 layers (not all 36), feature identification is fast (~2–3 GPU-hours). **Phase 2 — Entanglement-Aware Language Feature Anchoring (LFA) during GRPO**: Augment the GRPO objective with a tiered anchoring loss: L_total = L_GRPO + λ · L_anchor, where L_anchor combines two components based on the tier assignment: **Tier 1 (pure language features)**: L_tier1 = E_x[Σ_{s∈S_l^tier1} (f_s^θ(x) − f_s^ref(x))²] — standard MSE anchoring that preserves pre-training activation levels. These features can be strongly constrained because they carry language identity without reasoning function. **Tier 2 (dual-function features)**: L_tier2 = E_x[Σ_{s∈S_l^tier2} w_s · ReLU(proj_EN(f_s^θ(x) − f_s^ref(x)) − τ)²] — asymmetric directional anchoring that penalizes drift specifically toward English but allows within-language adaptation. Here proj_EN projects the feature drift onto the direction from target-language centroid to English centroid in feature activation space (computed from Phase 0 reference activations), and τ is a tolerance threshold allowing small drift. The weight w_s decreases with increasing reasoning_activation score, so highly dual-function features receive lighter anchoring. This formulation is motivated by the observation that cross-lingual collapse is directional (target → English), not random drift. **Tier 3 (pure reasoning features)**: unconstrained. L_anchor = L_tier1 + β · L_tier2, where β ∈ [0.3, 1.0] controls the relative weight of dual-function anchoring. **Why this differs from SASFT and simple MSE**: SASFT uses suppression (ReLU-based, push below threshold) at final layers during SFT. Simple MSE anchoring ignores entanglement and risks constraining reasoning-relevant features. LFA's tiered formulation leverages Phase 0's entanglement analysis to anchor strongly where safe (Tier 1), cautiously and directionally where needed (Tier 2), and not at all where unnecessary (Tier 3). The directional asymmetry in Tier 2 is novel: it recognizes that collapse is a specific failure mode (English attraction) rather than generic drift, targeting only the harmful direction of change. **Computational overhead**: The SAE forward pass at one layer costs ~537M FLOPs per token. At 2–4 target layers with backward pass, total overhead is ~3.2–6.4B FLOPs per token, approximately 7–13% of the gradient update step's compute. Since GRPO rollout generation (no SAE needed) is ~50–70% of total per-step compute, effective overhead is ~2–7% of total training cost. Optimizations: (a) compute L_anchor every M=4 gradient steps (reduces to ~0.5–2%); (b) cache reference activations; (c) sparse feature indexing. FPO (ICML 2025) validates this efficiency class. λ follows a warm-up schedule (0 for first 50 steps, linearly increasing to λ_max). **If Phase 0 reveals early-layer routing (alternative hypothesis)**: The method simplifies — early layers have minimal reasoning computation, so entanglement is low and standard MSE anchoring at Tier 1 features suffices. This is the simpler case, analogous to the original LFA design. **Phase 3 — Stratified Evaluation with Falsifiable Predictions**: We evaluate on MGSM (10 languages) and MGSM-Pro with explicit stratification: **High-resource (EN, ZH, DE, FR, ES, RU)**: Target >98% LC with <1pp accuracy degradation. **Mid-resource (TH, JA, KO)**: LFA's sweet spot. This poses a genuine risk that entity-level contrastive alignment may primarily improve same-script entity alignment while showing limited gains for cross-script pairs. EACA therefore incorporates a script-aware augmentation strategy: for cross-script QID pairs (e.g., EN-ZH, EN-AR, EN-HI, EN-TH, EN-KM), entity mentions in non-Latin scripts are supplemented with Latin transliterations appended within the [ENT] boundary (e.g., [ENT]北京 (Beijing)[/ENT]), providing a lexical bridge for the contrastive objective. This is tested as an ablation (EACA vs. EACA+translit) to isolate the contribution of transliteration augmentation beyond entity-level alignment. The evaluation plan includes mandatory script-grouped analysis: same-script entity alignment gains (Latin-Latin, CJK-CJK) vs. cross-script gains (Latin-CJK, Latin-Arabic, Latin-Devanagari, etc.), reporting both entity cosine similarity and downstream factual consistency metrics separately for each script-pair category. If Phase 0 reveals that cross-script entity alignment gains are <50% of same-script gains despite transliteration augmentation, this will be explicitly reported as a limitation and the analysis will quantify what fraction of EACA's overall conductivity improvement comes from same-script vs. cross-script alignment. 57 58 **4. Stratified Batch Construction with Type-Aware Hard Negatives.** Effective contrastive learning is highly sensitive to negative quality (Robinson et al., ICLR 2021). EACA uses stratified mini-batching: each batch contains K_batch = 128-256 unique QIDs, with all available language instances per QID forming the positive set (asymmetric positive sets accommodate QIDs present in only 2-3 languages without dropping them). Minimum language coverage per QID is K_min = 3 languages; QIDs with fewer than 3 language instances are filtered during preprocessing. Class-Aware Masking (CAM) ensures that all instances of the same QID are excluded from the InfoNCE denominator, preventing false-negative contamination. For hard negative mining, type-aware stratification ensures ~50% of in-batch negatives share the anchor entity's Wikidata type (e.g., Q5/human, Q515/city, Q4830453/organization) — forcing the model to discriminate on fine-grained entity identity rather than coarse type. This is implemented via Wikidata instance-of (P31) properties, grouping entities into 8-10 macro-types for sampling. The remaining ~50% are random negatives for diversity. Batch composition is balanced across script families to ensure cross-script contrastive signals appear in every batch. The InfoNCE loss for entity e with QID q is: L_entity(q) = -log[exp(sim(h_q^i, h_q^j)/τ) / (exp(sim(h_q^i, h_q^j)/τ) + Σ_{k≠q} exp(sim(h_q^i, h_k)/τ))], where h_q^i, h_q^j are entity representations from different languages for the same QID, and h_k are representations from different QIDs, with τ = 0.07 as the temperature (tuned in Phase 0 over {0.05, 0.07, 0.1}). 59 60 **5. Joint Optimization with Gradient Monitoring.** The joint objective is L_total = L_NTP + λ * L_entity_contrastive, with λ initialized at 0.1 (following guidance from headless LM work showing λ ∈ [0.01, 0.1] is appropriate for contrastive + generation joint training during CPT). A potential tension exists: NTP learns language-specific token distributions while contrastive loss pulls entity representations together across languages. Unlike Liu & Niehues' alternating approach, EACA uses joint optimization to ensure entity alignment co-adapts with the language modeling objective — but addresses gradient conflict risk through three mechanisms: (a) Phase 0 gradient analysis: cosine similarity between ∇L_NTP and ∇L_entity_contrastive is computed every 100 steps on the shared LoRA parameters. If gradient cosine similarity is negative for >30% of monitored steps, PCGrad projection (Yu et al., NeurIPS 2020) is applied — projecting the contrastive gradient onto the normal plane of the NTP gradient to eliminate destructive interference. (b) GradNorm (Chen et al., ICML 2018) is implemented as an optional dynamic λ adjustment mechanism: if the gradient magnitude ratio between the two losses drifts beyond 10:1, GradNorm normalizes to equalize learning rates. (c) λ warmup: contrastive loss weight ramps linearly from 0 to λ_target over the first 10% of training steps, allowing NTP to stabilize before contrastive pressure is introduced. Phase 0 reports gradient conflict frequency, cosine similarity distribution, and whether PCGrad/GradNorm activation was required — this informs the full training configuration. If gradient conflicts are severe (>50% of steps) even with PCGrad, the fallback is alternating optimization (NTP steps → contrastive steps per batch) following Liu & Niehues' validated approach. 61 62 Catastrophic forgetting is mitigated through three mechanisms: (a) LoRA (rank 64) applied to middle layers only (layers 10-22), following CCL-XCoT's selective layer approach and ELO's findings that first/last layers are critical for general capabilities; (b) 15% general-domain English replay data mixed into training batches; (c) cosine learning rate schedule with linear warmup (peak LR 2e-5). Language selection follows a tiered strategy: Tier 1 comprises 4 anchor languages (EN/ZH/JA/DE, >1M entity-fact pairs), Tier 2 includes 6 mid-resource languages (AR/HI/TR/ID/VI/TH, 100K-1M pairs), and Tier 3 covers 3 low-resource languages (SW/YO/KM). Tier 3 viability assessment based on Wikipedia article counts (SW: ~117K, YO: ~37K, KM: ~12K) and FactNet's 0.36 low-resource yield rate estimates approximately 50K-200K entity-fact pairs for Swahili, 15K-60K for Yoruba, and 5K-25K for Khmer. None of the Tier 3 languages are covered by DaMuEL, so all three rely on the Wikipedia wikilinks extraction pipeline (Stage 2 above). A mandatory FactNet coverage audit in Phase 0 will report exact entity-fact pair counts for all 13 languages; minimum viable threshold is set at 10K entity-fact pairs per language (sufficient for contrastive batching at size 128-256 with adequate negative diversity). If any Tier 3 language falls below threshold, contingency replacements include Bengali (BN, ~157K Wikipedia articles), Tagalog (TL, ~115K articles), or Hausa (HA, ~8K articles but stronger NLP benchmark coverage). Languages below 25K pairs receive LEIA-style English entity augmentation to supplement contrastive pairs. 63 64 Phase 0 pilot uses 500M tokens across 5 languages (3 Tier-1 + 2 Tier-2, selected to span at least 3 scripts for script barrier analysis) for approximately 130 H100 hours, with baselines including: (a) CCL-XCoT-style sentence-level contrastive CPT, (b) Liu & Niehues-style middle-layer sentence-level contrastive alignment (the closest methodological comparison, testing entity-level vs. sentence-level at the same middle layer), (c) LEIA-style entity augmentation without contrastive loss, (d) standard CPT, and (e) KBioXLM-style entity masking adaptation (masking [ENT]-bounded tokens and predicting via NTP, without contrastive loss — testing contrastive vs. masking-based entity alignment on decoders). Phase 0 additionally includes: a layer sweep (layers 12, 14, 16, 18, 20) to empirically determine optimal entity extraction depth; gradient conflict analysis (cosine similarity monitoring, PCGrad activation rate); and script-grouped entity alignment analysis (same-script vs. cross-script gains). Go/no-go criteria require entity cosine similarity improvement of at least 0.05, BMLAMA-53 consistency improvement of at least 2 points, no TyDiQA degradation beyond 1 point, AND gradient conflict rate below 50% (with or without PCGrad). Full training processes 1.5-2.5B tokens on LLaMA-3.1-8B (primary) and Gemma-7B (secondary, for CCL-XCoT comparability) across all 13 languages. A complementary EACA+DCO experiment tests whether pretraining-time and post-hoc consistency methods yield cumulative gains. Evaluation covers BMLAMA-53, TyDiQA-GoldP, X-CODAH, LiveCLKTBench, and CLiKA's XRR metric (to directly measure conductivity improvement), plus entity representation cosine similarity analysis. All metrics are reported with script-grouped breakdowns (same-script pairs, cross-script pairs, overall) as a mandatory analysis dimension.
